findings.message: "leaves something to be desired" equivalent: the phrase "is far from optimal" equivalent phrasing — "the picture for human visitors is strong" followed immediately by naming accessibility as a "Priority 1 compliance item" with 68 issues is not itself the problem, but the Executive Summary contains "Discovery Readiness sits at 25/100, the lowest score across the audit" which is neutral. However, the phrase "AI Suitability on served content scores 100/100 across the audited set, which is a strong foundations" contains a grammatical error ('foundations' should be 'foundation') that reads as a drafting error rather than a framing issue — not a category finding. The actual subtle-failure flag is in the Executive Summary: "Accessibility at 73/100 (Good) presents the clearest opportunity to close the gap" — this is acceptable opportunity framing. Scanning further: in the Balanced Scorecard narrative, "yet are constrained in their ability to discover" — 'constrained' is a subtle condemnation framing implying an active limitation rather than a neutral description of a low score.
findings.context: Balanced Scorecard > Machine Experience: "Across the audited set, machines can reliably parse and survive the content pipeline at 97/100, read structured signals at 63/100, yet are constrained in their ability to discover and index dotfusion.com purposefully, with Discovery Readiness at 25/100 and MX Stack Completeness at 44/100."

findings.message: The 'Next Steps > Recommended Actions' block item 2 reads: "Review Priority 2-3 findings: Catalogue Visibility improvements and metadata tuning that compound over time." This names only domain categories ('Catalogue Visibility', 'metadata tuning') with no specific element, page type, count, URL, or technical action. The phrase 'compound over time' is generic filler. The specificity test: the surrounding block (the entire Next Steps section) contains no data anchors — no scores, no URLs, no header names, no counts — that tie this recommendation to the audit findings. It could be copy-pasted unchanged into any web audit report.
findings.context: Next Steps > Recommended Actions, item 2: "Review Priority 2-3 findings: Catalogue Visibility improvements and metadata tuning that compound over time."

findings.message: Next Steps > Recommended Actions, item 3 reads: "Consider optional enhancements: optional patterns that give a early-mover opportunity in AI search." This names only a domain ('AI search') and a vague category ('optional patterns') with no specific element, mechanism, or data anchor. 'Early-mover opportunity' is marketing language. The specificity test: no data anchor appears anywhere in this item or its surrounding block. It could be inserted unchanged into any AI-readiness audit report.
findings.context: Next Steps > Recommended Actions, item 3: "Consider optional enhancements: optional patterns that give a early-mover opportunity in AI search."

findings.message: The llms.txt section states: "we recommend serving this file as text/html instead, because Common Crawl (the archive underpinning most major LLM training datasets) prioritises HTML for its LLM-training subsets, so a plain-text llms.txt is unlikely to enter training corpora at the same rate as the rest of the site." The claim that Common Crawl 'prioritises HTML for its LLM-training subsets' and the implied quantitative comparison ('at the same rate') are presented as established facts but are not sourced from the audit data, and the specific crawl-priority behaviour described is a characterisation of Common Crawl's internal processing pipeline that goes beyond a well-known binary fact. This introduces an unverifiable specificity into a client-facing recommendation.
findings.context: A note on llms.txt section: "Common Crawl (the archive underpinning most major LLM training datasets) prioritises HTML for its LLM-training subsets, so a plain-text llms.txt is unlikely to enter training corpora at the same rate as the rest of the site."

findings.message: Priority 1 recommends fixing unlabelled header anchor links by making "a single template edit" and verifying the fix "in the shared header template". The finding references the selector `#site-header`. While header navigation anchors could be first-party, the Pa11y finding pattern of zero-content anchor links in a site header on a Next.js site is a common symptom of icon-only links rendered by a component library or third-party navigation SDK injecting SVG icons without aria-label. The recommendation prescribes a template-level edit without investigating or acknowledging whether those anchor elements originate from a third-party component. However, because the selector `#site-header` does not contain any of the vendor-tell substrings defined in the check criteria, and the report does not confirm the elements are vendor-injected, this is borderline. Skipping — does not meet all three criteria definitively.

The Summary of Findings closes with: "We invite the dotfusion.com team to read on for prioritised recommendations that would close those gaps efficiently." The word 'efficiently' is not supported by any effort-estimate data in the audit; more importantly this is the end of the summary section, so 'read on' is directing the reader to content already above this section in the document. This is a structural incoherence (the reader has already read the findings) suggesting boilerplate copy was inserted without adaptation, but it is not an exaggeration finding. Not flagging under exaggeration. Flagging instead the genuine exaggeration: the Executive Summary states dotfusion.com is "a well-built property for the people it serves" immediately after noting 68 WCAG AA violations and a 73/100 accessibility score. Describing a site with 68 accessibility violations as 'well-built for the people it serves' overstates the human-experience baseline and reads as marketing softening rather than peer-to-peer consultant assessment.
findings.context: Executive Summary: "dotfusion.com is, in short, a well-built property for the people it serves." — stated immediately after noting 68 WCAG AA issues across the audited set affecting screen reader users.
